# The Phantasia-Orexis-Kinesis Circuit: Nussbaum's Interpretation of Phantasia in Animal Action 

## 1. As Nussbaum observes, "phantasia and desire are jointly necessary conditions for animal motion," and furthermore, "phantasia is a necessary condition for desire," which must "prepare" desire before the creature can be moved to act (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 10). This formulation is significant precisely because it establishes phantasia not as an ornamental or merely epiphenomenal capacity but as one that is structurally prior to desire itself in the causal chain of animal locomotion. What is at stake, accordingly, is an understanding of phantasia as the faculty that renders the perceptual world motivationally salient—that is, as a mode of "seeing-as" in which the object is apprehended under a description that can move the animal toward or away from it. Aristotle himself, in the *De Anima*, draws a fundamental distinction between two grades of phantasia: sensitive and deliberative., "Sensitive imagination, as we have said, is found in all animals, deliberative imagination only in those that are calculative: for whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation; and there must be a single standard to measure by, for that is pursued which is greater" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). This passage is crucial for understanding the stratification of animal life, since it implies that while all animals possess sensitive phantasia—the capacity to retain and respond to phantasmata even in the absence of the sensory object—only rational creatures are endowed with the deliberative form that permits comparison, measurement, and prospective planning. Indeed, Nussbaum emphasizes that phantasia is said to have "two sources: sense-perception or thinking," and that while its being (its *einai*) is different from any other faculty, it might still be "the same as" some other faculty in a qualified sense (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 22–24). The relationship between phantasia and belief (*doxa*) is thus a contested point; Nussbaum is careful to distinguish phantasia from mere opinion, noting that phantasia possesses an active, selective character that goes beyond passive reception. Furthermore, Nussbaum draws attention to the voluntariness and constructive dimension of phantasia. Our initial examination of the faculty, she notes, reveals that "it is because of the passive character of Aristotelian aisthesis that a further faculty is required agent's selective" engagement with the world (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 47). Perception, understood as *pathein*—a being-affected by the sensible object—is insufficient by itself to account for why one feature of the environment rather than another becomes the focus of the creature's practical orientation. Phantasia thus supplies what perception alone cannot: a selective, interpretive organization of the sensory field. This active dimension resonates with what Heidegger, in a different register, describes as being "affected by beings as world; πάσχειν as δέχεσθαι, 'to perceive' and that primarily as πάθος, 'becoming-affected,' 'disposition,' being related to the world as in it, being in dealings with it" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 277–280). The Heideggerian gloss helps illuminate why phantasia cannot be reduced to a mere copy of sensation; it is rather a mode of being disposed toward the world that makes motivating content available to the desiring soul. A fuller treatment of the internal distinctions within phantasia—particularly the question of whether deliberative phantasia introduces a genuinely new capacity or merely extends the sensitive form—will be developed in subsequent chapters; for now, it suffices to mark that phantasia operates as the interpretive hinge upon which action turns. 

## 2. Nussbaum on Orexis: Desire (ὄρεξις) If phantasia provides the motivating content—the "seeing-as" that renders an object desirable or fearful—then orexis is the faculty through which the creature is actually moved toward or away from that object. The phantasia-orexis relation is thus not merely sequential but deeply constitutive: desire cannot arise in the absence of a phantasma that presents something as good or harmful. Nussbaum is emphatic on this point, arguing that phantasia "must 'prepare' desire before" the animal can be moved, and that the two faculties operate as "jointly necessary conditions for animal motion" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 10). This joint necessity is philosophically significant, for it means that neither a bare representation without appetite nor a blind urge without representational content can issue in purposive locomotion. The circuit requires both elements working in concert. Aristotle's own account in the *Movement of Animals* reinforces this structure. "desire is the middle, and desire moves being moved," specifying that within "the animated body there must be some body of this kind" capable of serving as the instrument of desire's translation into physical displacement (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, pp. 9–11). The phrasing "desire moves being moved" is particularly revealing; it indicates that orexis occupies a genuinely intermediate position in the causal chain, neither purely active nor purely passive but rather a mediating force that is itself set in motion by the phantasma and that subsequently sets the bodily mechanism in motion. Thus the structure is triadic: phantasia furnishes the appearance of the good or the pleasant; orexis responds to this appearance with a directional impetus; and the body, through its organic constitution, executes the movement. Nussbaum's reading of this circuit highlights the way in which phantasia does not simply trigger desire mechanically but rather shapes its content. The creature does not merely see food; it sees something *as* food, and it is this "as-structure" that constitutes the phantasma's motivating power. Similarly, Heidegger's reading of (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) the *oὗ ἕνεκα*—the "for-the-sake-of-which"—is the primary respect in which beings show themselves, and that this teleological orientation is itself grounded in λόγος (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 160). The parallel is instructive: just as Heidegger reads Aristotelian teleology as a structure of disclosure in which beings appear within a totality of involvements, Nussbaum reads phantasia as the faculty that discloses the world under practical descriptions, thereby enabling orexis to fix upon determinate objects. The theoretical synthesis here is significant: to move a creature to action, an object must appear to it through selection, marking off, organization, and interpretation—precisely the functions Nussbaum assigns to phantasia in its relation to desire (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 22–24; Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). 

## 3. Nussbaum on Kinesis: Movement/Change (κίνησις) The third term of the circuit—kinesis, or movement proper—is the culmination of the phantasia-orexis sequence in actual bodily locomotion. Yet kinesis in Aristotle's technical vocabulary is not merely physical displacement; it carries the richer sense of the actualization of a potentiality, a passage from dunamis to energeia that is at once physiological and psychical. (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), the name energeia "came to be carried over to the other, to what contrasted with determinations of movement; ἐνέργεια, specifically, is related in itself πρὸς τὴν ἐντελέχειαν" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 213–215). This passage is illuminating for the question of animal movement because kinesis is not exhausted by local motion but participates in the broader ontological structure of actualization; the animal's movement toward food or away from danger is not merely a spatial event but the fulfillment of a practical potentiality disclosed by phantasia and activated by orexis. Nussbaum's account carefully attends to the physiological dimension of this process. "actual perception sets up certain motions (kinēseis) in the living creature, which persist in the absence of the object" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 39). These residual kinēseis are the material substrate of phantasmata—the traces left by perception that can subsequently be reactivated to motivate action even when the original sensory stimulus is no longer present. After his attempt to distinguish phantasia from other cognitive faculties, Aristotle, as Nussbaum explains, provides a theory of "motions (kinēseis) set up by actual perception, that remain even in the absence of the object and are 'similar' to the actual perceptions" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 41–43). The persistence of these motions is what allows the animal to act not merely in response to present stimuli but in light of past experience; the phantasma, as a residual kinesis, carries forward the practical significance of an earlier encounter into the present moment of action. Heidegger's reading of kinesis as a "how of being-there" rather than a separate entity further enriches this picture. "movement is not a being, but a how of being-there, such that the how of this there is something already present: look" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 266). Accordingly, the animal's locomotion is not an externally imposed displacement but a mode of its being-in-the-world—a way in which the creature exists among beings that have been disclosed to it through the phantasia-orexis circuit. Hence the practical syllogism, in which a major premise supplies a general desire and a minor premise supplies a particular perception or phantasma, issues not in a propositional conclusion but in an action—a kinesis that is the living body's response to the world as it has been opened up by phantasia. 

## 4. Nussbaum and Biosemiotic Dimensions The structural parallels between Nussbaum's reading of the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit and biosemiotic theory—particularly the work of Jakob von Uexküll—deserve careful consideration, even as they must be handled with appropriate caution regarding anachronism. Uexküll's concept of the *Umwelt*, the species-specific perceptual world of each organism, bears a striking resemblance to the Aristotelian notion that phantasia selectively discloses the environment in terms relevant to the creature's practical needs. As von Uexküll writes, "every subject spins out, like the spider's threads, its relations to certain qualities of things and weaves them into a solid web, which carries its existence" (von Uexküll, *Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans*, p. 53). This image of the organism spinning its own relational web captures something essential about the role Nussbaum assigns to phantasia: it is the faculty by which the creature does not merely receive sensory data but organizes that data into a practical field of significance. Nussbaum's analysis, while not explicitly invoking Uexküll, resonates with the biosemiotic framework insofar as she insists that phantasia supplies an interpretive organization of the sensory field—a "seeing-as" that goes beyond the mere registration of qualities to present objects under descriptions that motivate action. The phantasma, in this reading, functions analogously to what Uexküll calls the *Merkbild*—the perceptual sign or image through which the organism apprehends the functionally relevant features of its environment. Nussbaum observes that the "being (the einai) of phantasia is different from the being of any other faculty," suggesting its unique intermediary role (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 22–24). This irreducibility of phantasia to either raw sensation or abstract thought parallels the biosemiotic insistence that the organism's perceptual world cannot be reduced to the physicist's objective environment. Indeed, Aristotle's stratification of phantasia into sensitive and deliberative forms mirrors, to some extent, Uexküll's recognition that different organisms inhabit qualitatively different *Umwelten* depending on their sensory and cognitive endowments (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). 

## 5. Nussbaum and the Merkbild The concept of the *Merkbild*—the perceptual cue-image that an organism extracts from its environment and that guides its behavioral response—provides a particularly illuminating analogue for Aristotle's phantasma as interpreted by Nussbaum. Von Uexküll describes how each organism perceives only those features of its surroundings that are biologically significant, constructing a functional circle (*Funktionskreis*) in which the *Merkbild* triggers an effector response. "the environments that are as diverse as the animals themselves are offered to all animal subjects, not as a completed reality, but as mere potentiality for an individual construction" (von Uexküll, *Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans*, p. 126). This formulation—environments as potentiality rather than completed reality—aligns suggestively with Nussbaum's reading of phantasia as the faculty that actively constructs the motivating appearance from perceptual material, rather than passively receiving a ready-made representation. However, there are contested points where Nussbaum's reading diverges from alternative interpretations of phantasia's role. Scholars such as Wedin have argued for a more restricted, imagistic understanding of phantasia, treating phantasmata primarily as residual sensory images rather than as interpretive constructions with the rich "seeing-as" structure Nussbaum attributes to them. Nussbaum's response, implicit in her treatment, is that the Aristotelian texts themselves demand a broader reading: she points to passages where Aristotle "speaks of calculation about the future as though it involved a kind of picturing" and where "noëmata are included here alongside phantasmata," indicating that "Aristotle is not committing himself" to a narrowly imagistic account (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 53–55). This inclusion of noēmata alongside the faculty of phantasia, at least in its deliberative form, operates at a level of abstraction that exceeds mere mental imagery; it involves, rather, a structuring of experience under practical categories. The Uexküllian *Merkbild*, similarly, is not a photographic copy of an external object but a functionally selective extraction—a sign that condenses the organism's practical relation to its world. In this respect, the phantasma-as-Merkbild analogy illuminates a dimension of Aristotle's account that purely imagistic readings tend to obscure: the phantasma is always already oriented toward action, shaped by the creature's needs and capacities, and embedded within the totality of involvements that constitutes its lived environment. Heidegger's insight that beings are encountered not as "real things" independent of grasping but within a context of practical concern further supports this reading; he warns against acting on "reality" without having "seriously asked about it, and without showing which sense of being it possesses" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 270). Thus the phantasma, like the *Merkbild*, is never a neutral datum but always a practically constituted appearance—a disclosure of the world under the aspect of relevance for action. --- # VALIDATION APPENDIX ## Claim Map | # | Claim | Source | Page(s) |
